name: ulimit
description: A shell builtin that reports or sets per-process resource limits: open files, CPU time, memory, and processes.

flags.description: Open file descriptors (the famous "too many open files" limit).

examples.output:
core file size          0 blocks
open files              1024
max user processes      63345
examples.explanation: The full picture. open files 1024 is the classic default that breaks busy servers.
Raises the open-file limit for THIS shell and launches the server — the fix for "Too many open files" during testing.

examples.command:
user soft nofile 8192
user hard nofile 65536
examples.explanation: Persistent limits live in /etc/security/limits.conf (applied by PAM at login) or systemd LimitNOFILE= in unit files.

about: Limits are per-process, inherited from the parent, and enforced by the kernel. Soft limits can be raised up to the hard limit by the process itself; hard limits only root can raise. Three layers exist: shell ulimit, PAM limits.conf, and systemd unit directives — services get their limits from systemd, not your shell.
useCases: Fix "Too many open files" for servers.
Raise process limits for load testing.
mistakes: Setting ulimit in ~/.bashrc and expecting a systemd service to inherit it — services need LimitNOFILE= in the unit.
warnings: Raising limits without raising kernel-level capacity (fs.file-max, somaxconn) just moves the bottleneck.
